title: Ovonic threshold switch acts as one-device bitline comparator
idea: A room-temperature-sputtered chalcogenide OTS is biased just below threshold; the charge-shared bitline from a '1' pushes it over, and its snap-back delivers a large current pulse (near-infinite gain) captured by a 2-TFT latch, MINIFYING a ~12-transistor SA to ~3 devices.
why: Fact 7: SA area -70%; OTS threshold spread (~50 mV) must be trimmed per device, hence high risk.

title: Phase transition: insulator-metal switch replaces the cross-coupled latch
idea: TRIZ #36 Phase transition: a single NbO2 or VO2 threshold-switching element biased just below its insulator-to-metal transition sits on the sense node; the few extra millivolts from a stored '1' tip it abruptly into the metallic state, giving full-swing output from one device instead of a 4-6 transistor latch, and a reset pulse returns it to insulating.
why: Fact 7: sense-amp area could fall ~4x and fit the bitline pitch, and the abrupt gain tolerates smaller storage charge; threshold variability and thermal crosstalk are the risks.

title: Geiger-tube avalanche junction amplifies bitline charge
idea: Like a Geiger-Müller tube or a modern SPAD: one added implant mask forms a high-field p+/n junction at each sense node, biased just below breakdown, with the bitline voltage setting its reverse bias. The signal's sign decides whether impact-ionization multiplication (~10-50x) happens before the latch fires, and the junction is then quenched.
why: Charge gain at the sense node (fact 1) supports smaller cells or longer bitlines with ~2 extra devices per sense amp (fact 7).

title: SPAD-style avalanche first stage turns electrons into digital pulses
idea: LIDAR single-photon detectors get enormous gain from impact ionization; the SA first stage is an impact-ionization MOSFET biased just below breakdown, so a stored '1' (~1000 electrons) triggers a self-sustaining avalanche that is quenched and reset like a SPAD, while a '0' does not.
why: Gain ~1000x lets ~0.2 fF cells be sensed (fact 1); risks are dark-count false triggers and hot-carrier wear.

title: B: boron-doped avalanche junction as Geiger-mode bitline gain stage
idea: Place a tiny B/P-implanted p+n junction on each sense node, biased just below breakdown; the cell's few-thousand-electron surplus tips it into a self-sustaining avalanche (SPAD-style) that produces a rail-to-rail pulse, and an active quench transistor resets it in ~1 ns.
why: Gives digital-level output from a ~5 fF cell without a matched cross-coupled latch, potentially allowing Cs of 1-2 fF (fact 1) and smaller SAs (fact 7); risks are dark-count false triggers and breakdown drift with temperature.

title: V: vanadium dioxide insulator-metal switch as two-terminal comparator
idea: Bias a doped VO2 nanogap just below its insulator-metal threshold on each sense node; the cell's extra charge tips it metallic and hysteresis latches the result, replacing a 4-6 transistor latch with one two-terminal device. Doping shifts the 68 C transition above operating temperature.
why: SA area could fall ~3x (fact 7); the transition temperature and switching energy are open risks.

title: Antiferroelectric avalanche preamp multiplies femtocoulomb ferroelectric signals
idea: Constraint: non-volatile ferroelectric cells too small to give usable charge. At each SA input, a tiny antiferroelectric ZrO2 capacitor is biased just below its AFE-to-FE transition field; the cell's switching charge tips it over, releasing a large field-induced polarization step (~5-10x charge gain), and it relaxes back when the bias is removed.
why: Density: lets 3D-stacked FeRAM cells shrink to ~30 nm with ~1 fC signals, with charge gain built from the same HZO/ZrO2 toolset.

title: Bit-flip-aware training lets LLM caches run with zero ECC
idea: Box: cheapest cell x Si access x minimal SA x no ECC x bulk Si x standard. Models are trained and quantized with 1% random bit-flip injection on weights and KV-cache (bit-flip dropout, clamped exponent bits), then stored in uncoded relaxed DRAM where 1% flips act as regularization noise.
why: Removes all ECC parity and decode logic for AI tiers: +12% capacity and lower latency on top of relaxed-cell savings.

title: Chromatophore test pixels: optical wafer-wide readout of BIST results
idea: Cephalopod chromatophores show internal state on the skin. Each mat gets a tiny electrochromic (WO3/PEDOT) pad driven by its built-in self-test pass/fail latch. With power supplied through a few probe needles, a camera images the whole wafer during the BIST run and reads millions of mat results in parallel.
why: Testers cost millions and run for hours per wafer. Parallel optical readout could cut wafer-test time ~10x and shrink BIST/DFT I/O periphery, worth ~3-5% of cost per bit.

title: BEOL Schottky diode-matrix decoders minify predecode transistors
idea: Pd/IGZO Schottky diodes (<=300 C) wired as diode-ROM one-hot decoders above the array replace transistor predecoders, MINIFYING decoder transistor count ~10x and moving decode logic off the silicon.
why: Fact 7: row and column decoder silicon area -70%; reverse leakage in large fan-in diode matrices sets the size limit.

title: Eliminate silicon periphery footprint: n-only oxide-TFT dynamic logic above array
idea: Drop PMOS entirely and build decoders, wordline drivers and column logic from n-type oxide-semiconductor TFTs in the BEOL directly over the cell array, using bootstrapped domino-style NMOS-only logic with capacitive self-boost loads. Sense amps stay in silicon.
why: Moves ~30-40% of the periphery off the silicon footprint, shrinking the die ~25-35% (fact 7). Oxide-TFT leakage near 1e-19 A/um lets dynamic nodes hold for milliseconds.

title: Nanoelectromechanical relay row decoders and wordline drivers above the array
idea: Box: stacked cap x vertical Si access x conventional SA x BEOL-over-array decoders x Si x MEMS sacrificial release. Row decode trees and 3 V wordline drivers are built as electrostatic NEM relays (TiN beams, air-gap release) in the upper metal levels; relays have zero off-leakage and tolerate 3-5 V, so thick-oxide HV transistors leave the silicon.
why: Row decoder/driver area moves off Si (periphery -10-15% of die); HV driver standby leakage ~0. Relay endurance (needs ~1e15 cycles) is the open risk.

title: 2050 stacked periphery: four tiers of 2D-semiconductor sense amps
idea: A 2050 engineer builds periphery upward. Grow four monolithic BEOL tiers of MoS2 (n) and WSe2 (p) CMOS above the array; each tier hosts sense amps for one in four bitlines, relaxing SA pitch 4x and freeing the silicon footprint.
why: Moves most of the 49% periphery off the silicon footprint (fact 7) without hybrid bonding; relaxed pitch avoids EUV on periphery (fact 4).

title: Sample-and-hold capacitors let one sense amp serve eight bitlines
idea: Neural implants and image sensors time-share one converter across many columns; each bitline's post-charge-share voltage is captured on a BEOL MIM sample capacitor above the array, one SA resolves the eight samples in sequence, and a compact per-bitline write-back driver restores each cell.
why: SA count /8 and periphery area -15-20% (fact 7), at the cost of ~10-20 ns longer row cycle.

title: C: carbon nanotube sense-amp tier stacked above the array
idea: Print aligned semiconducting carbon nanotube films at <350 C on the bitline-contact level and build complementary CNT-FET latch sense amps and column muxes there, so the SA stripes move vertically over the mats instead of beside them. CNT's high mobility at 0.5-0.7 V keeps latch speed while the array below is untouched.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die (fact 7); lifting the SA stripes (~20% of die) above the mats could cut die area ~15-20% with a similar cost/bit gain and no litho node.

title: Transistor-free predecoders: threshold-switch diode matrix in BEOL
idea: Limit: decoders may use zero front-end transistors. Build predecoders as a BEOL crossbar of ovonic threshold switches and resistors above the array; the address bits applied to its columns make only one row's series OTS chain exceed threshold and snap on, firing that local wordline driver.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): ~6-9% of decoder silicon moves into stacked BEOL, with no extra EUV layers.

title: Ferroelectric negative-capacitance liner shrinks effective bitline capacitance
idea: Worse: make bitline capacitance as large as possible so the transfer ratio collapses. Flip: place a thin, stabilized ferroelectric layer in series within the bitline-to-neighbor spacer dielectric so its negative capacitance cancels part of the parasitic, lowering effective C_BL and amplifying the charge-sharing signal.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): signal ~ Cs/(Cs+CBL); halving effective CBL nearly doubles signal, allowing lower-AR capacitors or 2x longer bitlines with half the sense amps.

title: Lego studs: open standard for array-to-periphery bonded interfaces
idea: Lego bricks from any box snap together because the stud is standardized. Publish an open, royalty-free 'memory stud' spec covering bond pitch, per-bitline-group pad maps, voltage domains, test hooks and known-good-die protocol, so array-only wafers from any fab can bond to periphery wafers from any foundry; tie CHIPS-style funding to compliance.
why: Capital and supply diversity: breaks the 3-vendor vertical integration, letting U.S. logic foundries and new array specialists each enter with roughly half the capex of a full DRAM fab.

title: NMOS-only bootstrap wordline drivers revive 1970s DRAM tricks
idea: Early DRAM designers had no PMOS and drove wordlines with self-bootstrapped NMOS gates; reusing this, sub-wordline drivers need no PMOS or n-well, which removes well spacing from the SWD stripe and gives a uniform NMOS pitch printable with DUV.
why: SWD stripe area -25-35% (fact 7) and fewer masks.

title: Conductor's staggered entries: sense amps fire by section
idea: A conductor brings sections in one after another. Each row's sense amps are split into four groups fired ~300 ps apart within tRCD, flattening the peak current that bounces local ground and corrupts late-resolving SAs.
why: Cuts peak SA current ~4x and the ground-bounce share of the noise budget, letting SA devices shrink ~20% (fact 7).

title: Top-metal inductive coils over arrays replace HBM TSVs
idea: Substitute through-silicon vias with near-field inductive coil pairs drawn in top metal directly above the cell arrays, which use no silicon area. Stacked dies talk through face-to-back magnetic coupling.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes TSV keep-out zones and TSV-related yield loss (20-30%), cutting area per bit and stacking cost.

title: Inductive coupling coils replace TSVs between stacked dies
idea: MINIFY TSVs to zero for data: copper coils in each die's top BEOL (<=250 C) couple signals inductively to the dies above and below (ThruChip-style), so stacks need no TSV etch, fill or keep-out zones for data.
why: Fact 6: removes much of the TSV area tax and stack yield loss; power still needs a few TSVs or edge delivery.

title: TSV-free inductive-coil stack of headless DRAM dies
idea: Inverting 'stacked dies must be wired with TSVs': thinned dies talk through top-metal coil pairs (near-field inductive links, ~1 Gb/s per coil), power arrives by edge wire bonds, and only the bottom master die carries I/O, DLL and regulators while upper dies are headless arrays.
why: Avoids the HBM TSV tax (~3x wafer area per bit vs DDR5) and its 20-30% stacking yield loss while keeping wide internal bandwidth.

title: Fridge magnets: inductive coupling links replace TSVs in stacks
idea: Stick dies together like fridge magnets: replace HBM TSVs with on-die coils that couple data inductively between thinned stacked dies at ~1 Gb/s per coil and ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit, so no TSV keep-out zones or through-silicon etch are needed.
why: Die-to-die energy ~10x below today's TSV plus PHY paths, and removes the TSV area/yield tax (fact 6: ~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss).

title: Cu: electroplated copper coils link stacked dies without TSVs
idea: Replace HBM TSVs with inductive-coupling transceivers: spiral Cu coils, electroless-seeded and electroplated with no argon-sputtered barrier or seed, in each die's top metal pass data magnetically through 20-50 um of thinned silicon.
why: Eliminates TSV area, keep-out zones and TSV yield loss (fact 6, ~3x area per bit) at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit links.

title: Half the capacitor: negative-capacitance HZO preamp restores sense margin
idea: Limit: storage capacitor cut to 2.5 fF, so the bitline signal falls to ~40 mV. Place a series HZO ferroelectric layer in the gate stack of the sense amp's input pair, tuned to the negative-capacitance regime, so the internal gate swing is stepped up 2-4x before the latch regenerates.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): half the Cs lets pillar AR fall from ~70:1 to ~35:1, with cheaper etch and deposition and better yield, ~15-25% cost/bit. Risk: NC hysteresis and speed.

title: No global datalines: each subarray bonds straight to logic die
idea: Limit: no bank-level global I/O buses or secondary sense amps. Each subarray's SA stripe has its own local hybrid-bond pads (~0.5 um pitch, ~1e5 per die) that land directly on the logic or accelerator die, so data leaves through the shortest vertical wire.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and HBM TSV tax (fact 6): ~3-4 pJ/bit could fall below 0.5 pJ/bit, and global I/O area (~5% of the die) disappears.

title: Eliminate periphery from the DRAM fab: array-only wafers bonded per 32 bitlines
idea: Build the DRAM wafer with only cells, vertical access transistors and a 32:1 bitline mux made from the same vertical-channel devices. Each mux output lands on a 0.5-0.8 um hybrid-bond pad to a mature-node CMOS wafer that holds every sense amp, decoder, pump and I/O circuit.
why: Fact 7: the ~49% periphery area leaves the expensive DRAM wafer, and the DRAM flow drops its HKMG periphery and ~6-8 masks. Periphery can be built in U.S. 28-40 nm fabs; cost per bit -25-35%.

title: Ferreed-style latching microswitches for zero-standby bank gating
idea: Bell System's 1960 ferreed crosspoint used remanent magnetization to latch a reed contact, so it held its state with zero power. Build BEOL electrostatic microcontacts clamped closed by HZO remanent polarization, and use them to disconnect idle banks' periphery from the supply and to steer spare rows, with no holding power and no leakage when open.
why: Cuts periphery standby leakage in gated banks ~100x (idle power, fact 3 context) and replaces fuse-latch steering logic (fact 7).

title: Core-stack business model: periphery wafers from mature U.S. fabs
idea: Core memory was sold as a woven stack from one vendor and a driver/sense chassis from another. Split DRAM the same way: array-only wafers (cells and bitlines, no periphery) from existing DRAM fabs are hybrid-bonded to periphery wafers built on depreciated 28-40 nm U.S. logic lines, creating a merchant market for memory periphery.
why: Array dies gain ~1.6x bits per leading-edge wafer by shedding the 49% periphery (fact 7), and more of the value is made in the U.S. on existing tools (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Po: periphery made in a TV factory — LTPS glass chiplets
idea: Po: memory periphery from a display fab. Fabricate slow periphery (pumps, test, fuse/repair, ESD, power gating) as laser-crystallized poly-Si TFT circuits on Gen-6 glass panels, dice them into chiplets and bond them beside or under array dies.
why: Capital (#4) and U.S. manufacturability: panel lines process ~50x the area per tool-hour at a fraction of the cost per cm^2, and LTPS uses silicon only.

title: Array wafer carries only cells: periphery from U.S. legacy fabs
idea: Limit: the EUV array wafer may hold only cells and sense amps. Global decoders, pumps, I/O, DLL, test logic and fuses go on a 28/40 nm wafer from under-used U.S. legacy fabs and are joined by wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding at ~1 um pitch.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7), capital (fact 4), U.S. manufacturability: ~30% more bits per EUV wafer, with the periphery built on depreciated tools.

title: Eliminate row-hammer counter SRAM: leaky-capacitor analog activation integrators
idea: Replace the digital per-row activation counters (TRR/PRAC tables) with one analog integrator per 8-row group. Each ACT dumps a fixed charge packet, tapped from the wordline driver's own swing, onto a deliberately leaky MOS capacitor with a ~64 ms decay. When its voltage crosses a threshold inverter, the group's neighbors are refreshed.
why: Fact 9: protects at ~1k activations without counter SRAM/CAM (PRAC-style schemes cost several % of area plus timing). The integrator is 3 transistors per 8 rows, and its built-in decay matches the refresh window, so no reset logic is needed.

title: Printed oxide-TFT glass interposer performs die and bank selection
idea: Worse: repeat chip-select, rank and bank-group muxing logic inside every DRAM die and buffer chip. Flip: build a glass-panel interposer with inkjet-printed oxide TFT switches that set, per page epoch, which of dozens of simple array dies drive each high-speed lane, consolidating selection periphery into one cheap printed layer.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and capital: panel printing costs ~100x less per cm^2 than silicon, and array dies shed redundant control logic.

title: Thyristor-pair sense amplifier: T-RAM's latch reborn as periphery
idea: Failure mined: T-RAM died because a thyristor used as the storage cell had temperature-dependent holding current and standby leakage. Fix: use a cross-coupled gated-lateral thyristor pair as the bitline sense amplifier instead of the 6-8 transistor latch. It is biased only for the ~5 ns of sensing, so holding-current drift and standby leakage never matter, and its regenerative pnpn gain resolves ~20 mV in one step.
why: Periphery (fact 7): the sense-amp stripe is ~10-15% of the die. Two devices per bitline pair instead of 6-8 shrink it ~50-60% (~6% of die area back), and the higher gain tolerates a smaller cell signal.

title: Po: the sense amp remembers its offset — AlBN ferroelectric trim
idea: Po: a sense amplifier with memory. One input transistor of each SA gets a thin ferroelectric aluminum boron nitride gate layer; at test the measured offset is cancelled by one program pulse that permanently shifts that transistor's Vt, with no fuses or trim DACs.
why: Periphery (#7) and capacitor wall (#1): non-volatile per-SA offset cancellation lets SA devices shrink ~3x or cuts required signal ~40%, using Al, B, N instead of Hf-based HZO.

title: Tier-select transistor at each staircase step for 3D DRAM
idea: In stacked 3D DRAM, put a vertical oxide transistor at each staircase landing that acts as a tier decoder switch, so a few shared vertical wordline drivers fan out to N tiers through local selects; staircase contacts drop from N x rows to rows + N.
why: No manufacturable 3D DRAM (fact 2): staircase contacts and decoder area grow with tier count; this keeps periphery area nearly flat from 26 to 100+ tiers.

title: Delay-line regenerator: one fast sense amp services 64 dynamic bitlines
idea: Failure mined: mercury and magnetostrictive delay-line memories used one regenerating amplifier for thousands of bits and died only on serial access. Fix: in a 3D DRAM, the vertical bitlines hold their charge-shared signals dynamically for ~30 ns while one 20 GHz-class sense amp visits 64 of them through a fast mux, latching and restoring each in 0.4 ns. Row access stays random; only the sensing is serialized.
why: 10x at the same cost: SA area falls ~64x, so 3D DRAM breaks even at ~6-8 tiers instead of 26 (fact 2), and 48-64 tiers from shared etch steps give ~10x bits/mm^2.

title: Eliminate metal etch: pillar-first, catalyst-seeded electroless periphery wiring
idea: Photo-pattern an aminosilane SAM with UV-ozone and bind a Pd-ion catalyst only where lines and vias belong. Grow Co (with a Co-B cap) by electroless plating, build vias as plated pillars before the dielectric, spin-coat polysilazane-derived oxide over them, and polish to the pillar tops, so neither lines nor vias are ever etched.
why: Removes metal etch, via etch, fluorocarbon chemistry and Ta/W barriers from periphery BEOL; additive and few-tool, which suits the 60-200 nm periphery pitch.

title: Ga+N: gallium-nitride UV-LED maskless lithography for relaxed periphery
idea: Expose non-critical periphery layers (>80 nm pitch) with dense arrays of 365/280 nm GaN/AlGaN micro-LEDs imaged through reduction optics, with no mask, mercury lamp or neon excimer, letting each die's periphery be customized (for example per-bin repair routing) at exposure.
why: Removes masks and neon-dependent tools from about half of periphery layers (fact 4) and enables per-wafer customization.

title: Insurance pool: hashed global spare columns replace per-mat redundancy
idea: Like insurers pooling risk instead of every household holding reserves, remove the redundant columns from each subarray and give each bank a shared pool of spare column segments addressed by a small CAM keyed on (subarray, column), mapped in at the column path.
why: Periphery overhead: redundancy and fuse area (~3-6% of die) roughly halves, because statistical multiplexing needs ~5x fewer spares for the same yield.

title: Parameter change: 77 K operation lets junk polysilicon transistors stack 64-high
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change: memory sleds run immersed at 77 K, where leakage of cheap low-temperature polysilicon access transistors falls by ~1e6 and kT/C noise by ~4x, so 64 BEOL tiers of poly-Si 1T1C cells with planar ~2 fF capacitors hold data for minutes and are read by small low-offset cryo-CMOS sense amps under the array.
why: 100x path: 64 cheap tiers on a 40 nm logic base (~30x more bits per dollar of area), refresh periphery deleted, sense amps ~2x smaller; trade-offs: liquid-nitrogen infrastructure and ~10 W of cooling per W dissipated, so it suits rack-scale memory pools. Attacks Facts 2, 3 and 4.

title: Die-bank build-to-order: array dies stockpiled, 180 nm interface die added later
idea: Like Dell's build-to-order line, makers stockpile bare array dies (cells and SAs only). A U.S. assembler flip-chips each onto a 180 nm interface/periphery die chosen per customer (DDR, LPDDR, CXL, custom AI) when orders arrive, using 1990s C4 solder bumps and wide, slow buses.
why: Decouples scarce array capacity from interface churn, cuts inventory write-downs, and moves about a third of the memory value-add into U.S. mature fabs.

title: Lock-in detection of gain-cell current via modulated read wordline
idea: Gravitational-wave and lock-in instruments pull nanovolt signals out of 1/f noise by modulation; the read wordline is toggled at ~2 GHz for 8-10 cycles and the sense amp synchronously demodulates the bitline current with a mixer-integrator, so static offset and 1/f noise of the periphery cancel. Gain cells with read currents of only ~100 nA become sensible.
why: Lets weak, ultra-low-leakage gain cells (refresh-light, fact 3) work without big read transistors; SA offset requirement relaxed ~5x.

title: HDD servo wedges: embedded calibration rows retrim sense amps
idea: Like servo bursts written between data sectors on a disk, every mat holds a few known-pattern calibration rows; during refresh slots each SA reads them and steps a per-SA 4-bit trim capacitor until its offset is nulled, continuously in the background.
why: Periphery area: SA transistors can be near minimum size, since trim absorbs offset, shrinking the SA stripe ~30-40% and tolerating more Vt variation at small F.

title: Regenerative braking for wordlines via stepwise energy recovery
idea: Like an EV recovering energy while braking, discharge each 3 V wordline down a 5-step on-die capacitor ladder (stepwise adiabatic charging) instead of to ground, and charge the next wordline back up the same ladder.
why: Voltage floor/energy: wordline CV2 loss at ~3 V falls ~60-70% (N-step charging dissipates ~1/N), with less charge-pump load.

title: Lazy restore: defer write-back after destructive reads
idea: Inverting 'every read must immediately restore full charge': the sense amp releases the row once cells are ~70% restored and logs the row in a small weak-row table; the refresh engine tops those rows up within their shortened retention window, or immediately if the row is re-activated.
why: tRAS -30-40%, higher bank throughput and ~15% lower row-cycle energy with little added logic.

title: PLEDM gain-cell current lets 2048 cells share one sense amp
idea: Failure mined: Hitachi dropped its PLEDM gain cell (a vertical multi-tunnel-barrier transistor on a storage gate) when it exited DRAM. The overlooked strength was a current output that does not depend on bitline capacitance. Fix: hang 2048 PLEDM-style cells on one bitline with a current-integrating, auto-zeroed sense amp, instead of the 256-512 cells per charge-sharing bitline today.
why: Cuts the sense-amp count 4-8x (SA stripe from ~10-15% of the die to ~3%) and removes the bitline-capacitance limit on cell charge.

title: Other way round: column-first activation fires only requested wordline segments
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way round: instead of row-first (open 8 KB, then pick 64 B), the column address arrives first and is AND-ed with the main wordline at each sub-wordline driver, so only the 1-2 segments and local sense-amp groups under that column fire.
why: Fact 8: overfetch drops from 128x to ~2-4x and random-read energy from ~5.9 pJ toward ~0.3-0.6 pJ per useful bit; fewer opened cells also reduces row-hammer stress per access.

title: Trampoline: segmented plate-line bounce restores cells, bitlines swing 0.25 V
idea: Bounce the cell up from below like a trampoline: segment the normally common cell plate into per-row-segment plate lines; bitlines swing only ~0.25 V during sense, and restore happens by pulsing the segment's plate so the storage node is bootstrapped back to a full level through capacitive coupling, as in FeRAM plate-pulse schemes.
why: Bitline swing falls ~4x (energy ~4-8x) and restore charge moves through one plate segment rather than 8k bitlines; ~10x on array energy; risks are plate-to-plate coupling and disturb of unselected cells.

title: Child's take-turns sense amp: one latch scans eight bitlines
idea: A child asks why every bitline needs its own teacher. After charge sharing, isolation switches freeze each bitline's signal on its own bitline capacitance (it survives tens of ns), and one offset-cancelled latch visits 8 bitlines in ~1 ns steps, sensing and writing each back to full level in turn.
why: Periphery (fact 7): bitline sense-amp transistors drop ~6-8x, a ~10-15% die shrink; row cycle grows ~6-8 ns, acceptable for capacity tiers.

title: X-ray flat-panel charge integrators read centimeter-long bitlines
idea: Borrowed from flat-panel X-ray detectors, which read ~1 fC pixel charges down 40 cm data lines: each glass-panel bitline is held at virtual ground by a switched-capacitor charge-integrating amplifier, so the cell's full charge transfers to a small feedback capacitor whatever the line capacitance.
why: Charge wall on glass: the signal is set by Cs/Cfb instead of Cs/Cbl, so bitlines can be ~10x longer and sense amps per bit fall ~10x.

title: Putting-out system: 180 nm module hub does ECC, repair and refresh
idea: Like the pre-industrial putting-out system that sent specialized steps out to cottages, strip on-die ECC, repair maps, refresh scheduling and row-hammer tracking off every DRAM die. Put them in one 180 nm hub chip per module that runs wide and slow (e.g., 512 bits at 400 MHz).
why: On-die ECC and control logic take ~8-12% of die area; one hub per 8-16 dies removes that from every leading-edge die and adds U.S.-made content.

title: Polarity-swapping latches spread transistor stress evenly
idea: Ideal result: transistors that never age unevenly. Periodically invert each mat's stored polarity, tracked by one inversion flag bit, so every SA cross-coupled pair sees balanced BTI stress and offset drift never accumulates.
why: Offset drift otherwise eats ~5-10 mV of margin over life; recovered margin allows smaller Cs and longer service.

title: Ferroelectric HZO polarization stores per-amp offset trim
idea: Substitute large matched sense transistors with minimum-size FeFETs whose ALD HZO gate polarization is partially switched at test to null each amp's offset, so the trim is stored as analog polarization. HZO ALD, TiN sputter and RTA are standard nanofab tools.
why: Periphery area: offset-limited SA area shrinks ~3-5x once mismatch is trimmed instead of sized away.

title: Nanoelectromechanical relay decoders with zero off-state leakage
idea: Substitute CMOS decoder and wordline-isolation transistors with electrostatically actuated TiN or poly-Si NEM relays (sacrificial oxide release, e-beam gaps ~50 nm). Relays have truly zero off-current and abrupt switching.
why: Idle energy: removes decoder/driver subthreshold leakage, which dominates standby, and abrupt switching allows low-voltage decode logic.

title: Dopant-free undoped nanowire channels shrink sense-amp mismatch
idea: Substitute doped-channel sense transistors with undoped SOI nanowire gate-all-around devices whose Vt is set by gate work function (TiN/TaN), removing random dopant fluctuation. Oxidation thinning and e-beam patterning are university-standard.
why: Periphery area: sigma-Vt drops ~3x, so pitch-matched SA area shrinks up to ~5-9x (area scales with 1/sigma^2).

title: Sub-wordline driver doubles as row-wise back-gate bias generator
idea: Build access transistors with a buried back gate patterned per row, and merge the back-gate driver into the existing sub-wordline driver: idle rows sit at about -1 V back bias to choke the leakage tail, and the activated row flips to forward bias for stronger drive. One driver serves two gates, so no extra decoder is needed.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): a 150-200 mV effective Vt shift on idle rows could cut tail leakage ~10x (refresh 64 to ~512 ms); forward bias on the open row allows lower wordline voltage (fact 10).

title: C: amorphous-carbon nanorelay row decoders with zero leakage
idea: Replace local decoder and sub-wordline-driver transistors with electrostatic diamond-like-carbon cantilever relays built in BEOL; carbon-on-carbon contacts resist stiction and wear, and a relay's infinite off-resistance and abrupt pull-in pass the full 3 V VPP with no gate-oxide stress.
why: Sub-wordline drivers are a large, leaky slice of periphery (fact 7, fact 10); stacked relays could halve decoder footprint and drop driver standby leakage to ~0; ns-scale nanorelay switching fits a ~30 ns row cycle.

title: Po: rows only know 'next' — token-ring subarray refresh
idea: Po: a decoder that only knows 'next'. Add a display-style shift-register gate-driver chain (2-3 transistors per row, like gate-on-array in LCD panels) beside each subarray that passes a refresh token row to row, so idle subarrays refresh independently of the address decoder while others serve accesses.
why: Refresh (#3): hides the 10-20% bandwidth loss at 32-64 Gb through subarray-parallel refresh with ~1-2% area and no decoder contention.

title: No in-house analog team: open memory-periphery compiler for startups
idea: Limit: a new-memory startup gets zero analog designers. A CHIPS/DARPA-funded open-source periphery generator (sense amps, decoders, pumps, BIST) qualified on 28 nm and 22FDX U.S. processes lets array-technology teams design only the cell and tile it.
why: Capital and time-to-market: cuts ~18 months and ~$30-50M per new memory entrant, which widens U.S. supply diversity.

title: C: nanoporous carbon microsupercapacitors buffer activation current bursts
idea: Solution-cast nanoporous carbon electrodes with a gel electrolyte form a microsupercapacitor bank on the interposer or substrate under each DRAM stack, supplying the nC-scale ACT and refresh bursts so on-die decaps and VPP/VARY regulators can be ~3x smaller; processing is in air or N2, no argon sputter.
why: Decaps and regulators are a sizable part of periphery (fact 7); moving burst energy storage off-die frees area and steadies supply noise during sensing.

title: Active glass interposer with IGZO switches routes around bad dies
idea: MAGNIFY redundancy from cells to whole dies: a glass interposer carries IGZO TFT switch matrices (<=350 C) that remap channels from a failing HBM die or TSV column to a spare die in the stack, configured at final test.
why: Fact 6: recovers much of the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss; glass panel substrates are cheap and a U.S. manufacturing strength.

title: Liquid-CO2 garment dry-cleaning for periphery post-etch residue
idea: Dry cleaners replaced perchloroethylene with liquid CO2. Clean every periphery post-etch and post-ash step with supercritical CO2 plus 1-3% alcohol/amine cosolvent in a pressure chamber that recaptures >95% of the CO2, keeping one short single-wafer UPW rinse only before the gate.
why: Water: ~30-40 periphery residue cleans each drop from ~10-20 L UPW per wafer to near zero, ~10x less for the module; relaxed periphery pitch makes scCO2 penetration easy.

title: Charge-trap access transistor captures each cell's bit at shutdown
idea: Constraint: non-volatile with zero added cell area. The access transistor's gate stack includes a nitride trap layer; at power-fail, bitlines float and a high wordline pulse lets each storage node's own potential (0 or 1 V) set the drain-edge field, injecting charge asymmetrically; at power-up SAs sense the Vt shift by reverse-reading through a gate ramp, then rewrite the capacitors.
why: Per-cell NV backup in the existing footprint (no backup layer). Risk: write disturb and program margin from a 1 V difference.

title: Phase-encoded parametron cells read by frequency multiplexing
idea: Inverting 'every bit needs its own wire to a sense amp': bits are the 0 or pi phase of parametrically pumped nanomechanical resonators, each tuned to a distinct frequency, so one shared readout line and one phase-detecting receiver demodulate 32 cells at once.
why: Sense-amp count drops ~32x and the pump keeps each bit alive continuously instead of by refresh; attacks periphery area and leakage, but is speculative on density.

title: ECC syndromes trigger background column remapping
idea: Ideal result: a memory that fixes faults before anyone notices. On-die ECC logs syndromes per column in a small nonvolatile table; repeat offenders are remapped to spare columns online, with data copied during refresh idle time.
why: Keeps parts in service and cuts module returns; periphery repair happens continuously in the field.

title: One sense die multiplexed across four headless array dies
idea: Inverting 'every array owns its periphery': four stacked array dies carry only a one-transistor local preamp per bitline group, and a single logic die underneath holds the latching sense amps, decoders and I/O, selecting which die's preamps drive the shared vertical hybrid-bond column buses like a bank select along the z-axis.
why: Amortizes the ~49% periphery over four arrays so array dies are ~90% cells; stack-level cost per bit -30-40% and only one die needs logic-grade transistors.

title: Completion-detecting self-timed sense amps remove worst-case guard bands
idea: Asynchronous circuits built for deep-space radiation and 30-year aging corners signal when they are done; dual-rail SA outputs feed a completion tree per mat that fires column access as soon as every latch has resolved, instead of waiting a fixed tRCD set by the slowest cell at end of life.
why: Typical-case row-to-column latency 20-35% lower; timing margin recovered as bandwidth, so the 49% periphery (fact 7) does more work.

title: Na: sodium-ion glass integrator counts each row's activations
idea: Attach to each row driver a tiny Na+-conducting glass cell encapsulated in SiN; every ACT pulse pushes a fixed quantum of Na+ across it, raising its conductance, and when a comparator crosses threshold the controller refreshes the neighbors and resets the cell with a reverse pulse.
why: Exact per-row counting today needs SRAM/CAM tables that balloon as the row-hammer threshold falls to ~1k (fact 9); an analog ionic counter under each driver costs ~no SRAM and gives deterministic protection.

title: Magnify mat size with mid-bitline charge-transfer preamplifiers
idea: MAGNIFY bitlines from 512 to 2,048 cells by inserting a charge-transfer (Heller-type PMOS) preamplifier at the midpoint that moves far-segment charge onto a small node with gain, halving the number of SA stripes and decoder columns per bit.
why: Fact 7: SA plus decoder overhead per bit -25-30%, periphery share toward ~38%; a 1990s trick reused for a periphery-bound era.

title: LC-resonant adiabatic driver chiplet recycles command/address bus energy
idea: Effect: LC resonance energy recovery. A small mature-node chiplet drives the DRAM command/address and clock nets as part of an LC tank (on-package inductor plus net capacitance), so energy sloshes between the inductor and the wires instead of being dumped as CV^2 on every toggle; commands are encoded by pulse position on the resonant waveform.
why: Data-movement/periphery energy (fact 5): CA and clock bus energy cut ~60-75%; MPW plus OSAT only.

title: Williams-tube pickup plate: segmented cell plate becomes the sensor
idea: The Williams tube read every spot through one pickup plate over the tube face. One added plate-cut mask divides the common cell plate into tiles, each wired to a charge amplifier in the CMOS under the array. When a cell is accessed, its charge redistribution appears on its tile, so one amplifier per tile can read any cell for scrubbing, retention profiling and low-bandwidth reads without firing the bitline sense-amp row.
why: Background operations skip the 8 kb page activation, ~100x less energy per scrubbed bit (fact 8), and enable per-row adaptive refresh (fact 3).

title: HMC's SerDes replaced by sense amps driving TSVs directly
idea: Failure mined: Micron's Hybrid Memory Cube lost on SerDes power and cost. Fix: each bank's secondary sense amps drive their TSV with a 100-150 mV charge-domain swing straight to a strobed latch on the base die. This deletes the DRAM-side global I/O lines, data buffers, serializers and DQ drivers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~0.5-1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM, and ~8-10% of the DRAM die's periphery is deleted.

title: Isolated early-latch sensing with parity-checked deferred restore
idea: Worse: wait for every bitline to fully develop under worst-case corners before latching. Flip: latch at half the usual development time with isolation gates cutting the latch off from the bitlines, ship data out, and write back only after a per-burst parity check passes; on a rare mismatch the still-intact shared bitline charge is re-latched with more time.
why: Latency, bandwidth and read energy: ~30% lower tRCD at typical corners while keeping worst-case correctness.

title: Snap-through buckled-beam NEMS crosspoint: bistable, contactless, self-selecting
idea: Failure mined: the first-generation NEMS memories from Cavendish Kinetics and Nantero died on stiction and contact wear. Fix: a pre-buckled 40 nm nanobeam over each crosspoint snaps between two stable shapes without touching anything. Snap-through has a sharp voltage threshold, so half-selected cells never flip, and the state is read as differential capacitance to the row and column electrodes.
why: 10x at the same cost: transistorless 4F^2 cells with built-in selection, unlimited contactless endurance and zero leakage (no refresh). Four sacrificial-release decks sharing lines, plus minimal periphery, give ~10x bits per wafer cost.

title: Row-granular decompressor in the sense-amp stripe, after IBM MXT
idea: Failure mined: IBM's MXT compressed main memory died on decompression latency and a costly controller far from the DRAM. Fix: put a wide, row-granular decompressor (zero-run coding plus 4-bit quantization tables for AI weights, KV caches and activations) right after the secondary sense amps. Its work overlaps the activation's tRCD and rows are stored compressed, so effective capacity multiplies with no added latency.
why: 10x effective density at the same cost for AI data: 4:1 quantization x ~2.5:1 sparsity and zero-run coding = ~10x usable capacity per bit cell. It also cuts data-movement energy (fact 5) ~10x per useful value, for ~3% of die area.

title: Motion-sensor porch light: clockless periphery wakes only on command
idea: A porch light stays dark until someone walks up. Remove the always-on DLL and replace it with source-synchronous strobes, bias command receivers only when chip-select toggles, and replace idling charge pumps with reservoir capacitors recharged right after each burst, so the periphery draws near zero between accesses.
why: At 10-30% utilization, background power (DLL, receivers, pumps) is 40-60% of energy per access; making it event-driven cuts energy per access ~3-10x for lightly loaded memory tiers.

title: Feedback: shared sigma-delta loops read three bits per cell
idea: TRIZ #23 Feedback: after charge sharing each bitline holds its voltage on its own capacitance while one 1-bit sigma-delta modulator per 128 bitlines visits them in turn, feeding back charge packets until balanced, resolving 8 charge levels (3 bits) per planar cell in ~2 us instead of a binary latch per bitline.
why: 100x path: 3x bits per cell and 128x fewer sensing circuits, compounded with stacked mature-node tiers; trade-offs: microsecond reads, cells must hold ~8x finer charge levels so leakage must be very low (oxide TFTs), and refresh must rewrite multilevel values. Attacks Facts 1 and 7.

title: Steep-slope tunnel-FET sense amps enable 0.5 V array voltage
idea: Substitute MOSFET sense pairs with heterojunction tunnel FETs (~30 mV/dec) used only in the latch, where low drive current matters less, so the array voltage drops from ~1 V to ~0.5 V while the latch still regenerates.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): array CV^2 falls ~4x; leakage at low VARY also falls.

title: Tunnel-FET input pair inside a conventional MOSFET latch
idea: Replace only the input pair of the DRAM sense amp with steep-slope tunnel FETs (sub-60 mV/decade) and keep MOSFETs for restore, so the latch begins amplifying at VARY ~0.5 V, where MOSFET-only latches barely turn on.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): halving VARY cuts bitline CV^2 energy ~4x, and refresh energy falls with it.

title: Dirac-source steep-slope sense transistors at 0.4 V
idea: Low-temperature (<=400 C) MOCVD MoS2 channels with a graphene cold-source contact that filters out high-energy electrons give sub-60 mV/decade switching, letting SAs and the array MINIFY VARY to ~0.4 V.
why: Fact 10: CV2 array energy -80%; low-temperature 2D growth quality and contact resistance make it speculative.

title: Passive-house memory: tunnel-FET latch sensing at 0.35 V
idea: Passive houses skip HVAC by cutting the heat load at the source. Run the array at VARY 0.35 V and sense with a cross-coupled tunnel-FET latch (steep <40 mV/dec slope keeps gain at low voltage), cutting bitline CV2 ~8x so modules stay within air-cooling heat flux and racks need no evaporative cooling for memory power.
why: Lifecycle water/energy: DRAM is 20-30% of server power; ~8x less array energy plus air cooling cuts the evaporated cooling water attributable to memory (~1-2 L/kWh) ~10x and breaks the voltage floor.

title: Selective assembly: pick the best-matched transistor fingers per sense amp
idea: As engine plants pair pistons with bores by measured size, build each SA input side from four half-width candidate fingers. At test, e-fuse switches keep the finger pair whose Vts match best, the way 1990s analog chips trimmed matched pairs.
why: Best-of-4x4 selection cuts offset sigma ~2-3x without advanced litho, so bitlines can double in length; net SA area falls ~20-30% even at 180 nm.

title: Off-die replaceable voltage-generation chiplet powers memory periphery
idea: Ideal result: the memory die holds no pumps or regulators that wear out. Move VPP, VBB and VARY generation to a socketed power chiplet on the module that feeds dies through dedicated rails; failing or outdated regulators are swapped, and the chiplet is reused on new modules.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): frees several percent of die area from charge pumps and makes the highest-stress periphery repairable.

title: Stack-level erasure coding rescues HBM stacks with one weak die
idea: Box: standard cells x Si access x per-die soft SA x cross-die erasure code in base die x Si x TSV stacking. Each codeword is spread across all 12-16 dies of an HBM stack, so a die with ~1% bad cells or a weak TSV group counts as a partial erasure instead of scrapping the stack.
why: HBM TSV tax: most of the 20-30% stack yield loss recovered; effective HBM supply +15-25%.

title: Pin-factory split: tiny per-pair preamps, shared high-voltage restore drivers
idea: Adam Smith's pin factory split one job into specialized steps: split the SA into a minimal thin-oxide preamp per bitline pair that only decides and holds the bit, plus one strong restore driver shared by four pairs. The shared driver writes full-swing values back in four ~3 ns phases within tRAS.
why: Restore devices are the largest part of the SA; sharing them 4:1 cuts SA-strip area ~30-40% and lets the preamp use smaller, better-matched devices.

title: Gate-on-array shift register walks refresh through wordline strips
idea: Borrow the LCD gate-driver-on-array (GOA) shift register: a ring of two-transistor shift stages embedded in each sub-wordline driver strip passes a refresh token row to row, so refresh activates rows without powering the refresh address counter, the predecoders or the global row bus.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): strips decode and global-wire energy (~30-40% of per-refresh energy) out of every refresh, sharply lowering self-refresh power.

title: Randomly coded nanowire decoders mapped after fabrication
idea: Substitute lithographically exact decoders with an e-beam nanowire array whose gate oxide is randomly modulated (random doping or random dielectric patches). After fabrication a tester discovers each wire's address code and stores the map.
why: Litho and capital (fact 4): decoders can sit at sub-litho pitch without alignment, tolerating defects through discovery instead of precision.

title: Monument laser cleaning: shock-wave particle removal before periphery contacts
idea: Conservators clean cathedral stone with pulsed lasers and no water. A nanosecond laser flash-heats the wafer surface so thermal expansion and the gas-film shock wave lift particles from periphery contact/via openings, and a nitrogen cross-flow sweeps them into an exhaust, replacing megasonic DI-water scrubs.
why: Water: periphery particle scrubs (~10-20 L UPW each) fall ~10x, and dry removal has no capillary pattern-collapse risk.

title: CHIPS-funded open DRAM periphery IP for every U.S. fab
idea: Reverse the IP model: a government-funded consortium publishes silicon-proven SA, decoder, pump and PHY hard macros with layouts for U.S. mature and memory fabs as open IP, so periphery becomes public infrastructure and companies compete on arrays.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: periphery is ~40-50% of new-DRAM design cost; lowers entry for U.S. memory startups.

title: Eliminate the isolation trench: grow periphery isolation by area-selective ALD
idea: Skip the fluorocarbon STI etch and the HF liner and oxide strips. Non-fluorinated alkyl-aminosilane inhibitor SAMs mark the device islands, and repeated inhibitor-refresh cycles of area-selective ALD grow ~80 nm Al2O3 isolation ridges only between them. Selective Si epitaxy (dichlorosilane/HCl) then raises the active areas level.
why: Removes the whole STI module (trench etch, liner, fill, heavy CMP) and every fluorine step in isolation; periphery front-end cost ~-30%.

title: ARM-style IP licensing of thin-film periphery to display fabs
idea: Borrowed from ARM's licensing model: develop a validated library of oxide-TFT sense amps, decoders and pumps (with process recipes) and license it to underused Gen-6/8.5 display fabs for a royalty per square meter, so memory supply grows with existing panel capacity.
why: Supply and capital: taps tens of millions of m2 per year of display capacity without new fabs and turns periphery design into a reusable asset.

title: Latch resolution-time monitor flags weakening cells before they fail
idea: Effect: exponential regeneration in a bistable latch (metastability). Standard-cell time-to-digital counters on a few sense amps per mat measure how long each latch takes to resolve; since resolution time grows as tau*ln(Vswing/dV), a slow decision reveals a cell whose charge is nearing the trip point, and the controller raises refresh only for that row.
why: Refresh (fact 3): sensed per-row margins replace worst-case refresh (~50% fewer refreshes) and catch variable-retention drift online; MPW-buildable.

title: Hadamard-coded multi-row reads give tiny MRAM signals root-N SNR
idea: Constraint: non-volatile resistive cells with weak signal. Because MRAM reads are non-destructive, activate N rows at once with +/-1 Hadamard-coded read biases over N sense cycles and invert the code in a small digital block; the Fellgett multiplex advantage gives a sqrt(N) SNR gain per cell (4x at N=16).
why: MRAM sensing margin (low TMR) drives large SAs and references; sqrt(N) lets read current fall 4x (less read disturb) or the SA shrink, and it tolerates lower-TMR, cheaper stacks.

title: Bitline segments become a SAR DAC for two bits per cell
idea: Rearrange the bitline into a capacitive DAC: it is cut into binary-weighted segments switched in successive-approximation steps around the SA, resolving four charge levels per cell in two comparisons, with restore through the same segments.
why: Density x2 with no new cell and no separate DAC area; per fact 1 the margin is tight, so it pairs with offset cancellation or larger Cs.
